response: {"text":"A set of nonlinear differential equations describing the electrical behavior of a large nerve fiber were examined using graphical techniques and a hardware simulation device. The membrane voltage and the activation variable for sodium change quickly, while the sodium inactivation and potassium activation evolve more slowly. By fixing the slow variables at their resting levels, the two‑dimensional plot of voltage versus sodium activation shows three equilibrium points: a stable resting state, an unstable threshold (saddle) and a stable excited state. Allowing the slow variables to move causes the threshold and excited points to shift and eventually vanish, producing the observed recovery and refractory periods. Lengthening the time constant of the potassium activation by a factor of about one hundred and shortening that of the sodium inactivation to roughly one third reproduces the long‑lasting depolarizations seen experimentally when a particular potassium‑blocking drug is applied, including the loss of excitability and the dependence of the plateau on its duration.
